overview.heading: International Optimist
overview.text: A small sailing dinghy for one sailor, up to the age of 15. Clark Mills designed it in 1947 in Florida, and today young sailors race it in well over 100 countries. Every Optimist is built to the same rules, so races are won by the sailor, not the boat.
overview.hint: Click any part of the boat or pick one from the list. Drag to look around, scroll or pinch to zoom. Move the boom slider to change course against the wind.

hull.name: Hull
hull.text: The body of the boat. The Optimist has a flat bottom and two flared sides that meet at a sharp edge called the chine. This wide, boxy shape makes it very stable, which is why so many sailors start in one.

bowTransom.name: Bow transom
bowTransom.text: The Optimist has no pointed bow. The front is a small, flat, sloping panel called a pram bow. It keeps the boat short but roomy inside.

sternTransom.name: Stern transom
sternTransom.text: The flat back wall of the boat. The rudder hangs on two fittings here, and the aft buoyancy bag sits against its inside.

gunwale.name: Gunwale
gunwale.text: The rolled top edge of the hull (say “gunnel”). It makes the sides stiff, and it is where you sit and lean out to balance the boat.

rubbingStrake.name: Rubbing strake
rubbingStrake.text: A tough strip around the outside of the gunwale. It protects your boat, and other boats, when you bump into a pontoon or each other.

mastThwart.name: Mast thwart
mastThwart.text: The strong crossbeam near the bow. The mast goes through the hole in the middle. The bulkhead under it stiffens the front of the boat, and the painter is tied here.

mastStep.name: Mast step
mastStep.text: The socket on the floor where the bottom of the mast (the heel) sits. It can be moved a little to tune the mast rake, but never during a race.

midshipFrame.name: Midship frame
midshipFrame.text: A frame across the middle of the boat that keeps the hull stiff. The daggerboard case is built into it, and the toe straps are fixed to its back.

daggerboardCase.name: Daggerboard case
daggerboardCase.text: A narrow box in the middle of the boat, open at the bottom. The daggerboard slides down through it into the water, and the water stays out.

buoyancy.name: Buoyancy bags
buoyancy.text: Three air bags: one on each side and one across the stern. If you capsize, they keep the boat floating high so you can pull it upright and sail on.

toeStraps.name: Toe straps
toeStraps.text: Two padded straps along the floor. Hook your feet under them to lean out over the side (hiking) and keep the boat flat in strong wind. A shock cord lifts them so your feet find them easily.

gudgeons.name: Rudder fittings
gudgeons.text: Two gudgeons (eyes) on the transom and two pintles (pins) on the rudder. The pins drop into the eyes so the rudder can swing. A clip stops the rudder falling off if you capsize.

mast.name: Mast
mast.text: The upright pole that carries the sail. No wires hold an Optimist mast: it stands on its own in the thwart and the step. The two black bands near the top show how high the sail may go.

boom.name: Boom
boom.text: The pole along the bottom of the sail. It swings across the boat every time you tack or gybe, so keep your head down!
spec: The clew may not pass it

boomJaws.name: Boom jaws
boomJaws.text: The fork at the front of the boom that hugs the mast. A short line goes around a pin on the mast so the boom cannot slide up.

sprit.name: Sprit
sprit.text: The thin pole that runs diagonally across the sail. It pushes the top corner (the peak) up and back, which makes the Optimist a sprit rig. Rig it on the starboard side.

windIndicator.name: Wind indicator
windIndicator.text: A small vane on top of the mast that points into the wind. Move the boom slider and watch it turn as the wind direction changes.

sail.name: Sail
sail.text: A four-sided sail of about 3.3 m². It is tied to the mast and boom and held up at the top by the sprit. Wind flowing over its curved shape pulls the boat along.
spec: 8 on the luff, 8 on the foot

luff.name: Luff
luff.text: The front edge of the sail, tied to the mast at 8 eyelets. Pull these ties tight so the sail stays close to the mast.

leech.name: Leech
leech.text: The back edge of the sail. Nothing holds it, so two battens help it keep a smooth shape.

foot.name: Foot
foot.text: The bottom edge of the sail, tied to the boom. Leave these ties a little loose so the sail can form a smooth curve.

head.name: Head
head.text: The top edge of the sail, running from the throat up to the peak.

tack.name: Tack
tack.text: The bottom front corner of the sail, where the mast and the boom meet.

clew.name: Clew
clew.text: The bottom back corner of the sail. The outhaul pulls it toward the end of the boom.

throat.name: Throat
throat.text: The top front corner of the sail. It is lashed through two holes at the top of the mast.

peak.name: Peak
peak.text: The highest corner of the sail. The top of the sprit fits into a loop here and pushes it up.

battens.name: Battens
battens.text: Two stiff strips in pockets on the leech. They stop the back edge of the sail from curling or flapping.

window.name: Window
window.text: A clear panel low in the sail. Look through it for boats hidden behind your sail.

sailNumber.name: Sail number
sailNumber.text: The country letters (BUL is Bulgaria) and the boat’s own number. On the starboard side the number is in the upper row, on the port side in the lower row, so the two sides do not cover each other.
sailNumber.note: This boat is BUL 1947: the year Clark Mills designed the Optimist.

daggerboard.name: Daggerboard
daggerboard.text: A flat board pushed down through the case. Under water it stops the boat sliding sideways, so you can sail across the wind and even toward it. Lift it part of the way when the wind is behind you.
daggerboard.note: The wooden stop battens at the top stop it dropping through the case.

rudder.name: Rudder
rudder.text: The blade at the back that steers the boat. It turns on its pintles and you move it with the tiller.

tiller.name: Tiller
tiller.text: The handle fixed to the top of the rudder. Push it away from you and the boat turns toward the wind. Pull it toward you and the boat turns away.

tillerExtension.name: Tiller extension
tillerExtension.text: A hinged stick on the end of the tiller, so you can steer while sitting out on the side. Most sailors hold it across the body, like a microphone.

mainsheet.name: Mainsheet
mainsheet.text: The rope that controls the boom. Pull it in when you sail toward the wind; let it out when the wind comes from behind. You always hold it in your hand.

blocks.name: Blocks
blocks.text: Pulleys that guide the mainsheet from the boom down to the floor. The ratchet block lets the rope run out easily but grips it while you hold it, so your hand gets less tired.

vang.name: Vang (boom downhaul)
vang.text: A line that pulls the front of the boom down toward the mast. It stops the boom lifting and controls the shape of the top of the sail.

spritHalyard.name: Sprit halyard
spritHalyard.text: The line that holds the lower end of the sprit on the mast. Tighten it to push the peak up and take out the diagonal crease in the sail. Ease it in light wind.

outhaul.name: Outhaul
outhaul.text: A short line that pulls the clew toward the end of the boom. Tight makes the sail flatter for strong wind; looser makes it fuller for light wind.

sailTies.name: Sail ties
sailTies.text: Short cords that tie the sail to the mast and the boom, one at each eyelet. Tie them with a reef knot: tight on the mast, a little loose on the boom.

painter.name: Painter
painter.text: The bow line: at least 8 m of rope that floats. Use it to tie up the boat or to be towed. Keep it coiled so it never trails in the water.

daggerboardRetainer.name: Daggerboard elastic
daggerboardRetainer.text: The elastic holds the daggerboard at the height you choose. The lanyard keeps the board attached to the boat if you capsize.

bailer.name: Bailer
bailer.text: A scoop, often a cut-down plastic bottle, for throwing water out of the boat. It must be tied on.

paddle.name: Paddle
paddle.text: For when the wind dies, or to get out of trouble. It is tied to the boat so it cannot float away.

compass.name: Compass
compass.text: Optional. Racers use it to notice when the wind changes direction, called a wind shift.
